seoTitle: Multiple Correct Answers in Microsoft Forms Quizzes
metaDescription: Learn how to let quiz-takers pick more than one correct choice in Microsoft Forms, assign points, and grade the combination automatically.
intro: Single-choice questions fall short when a quiz needs more than one right answer, whether you're certifying technical skills or grading a compliance test. This guide shows how a plain Multiple Choice question in Microsoft Forms converts from radio buttons to checkboxes the moment you flip on Multiple Answers, and how the Select total options setting lets you control exactly how many boxes a respondent is allowed to check. It's grounded in the actual question-builder screens, not just the toggle names.

steps.heading: Start with a fresh Multiple Choice question
steps.body: Add a new question and choose the Multiple Choice type, and by default it behaves like a normal single-answer question — each option gets a round radio button, meaning only one can be selected at a time. Below the option list sit two toggles side by side, Multiple answers and Required, both switched off at this starting point. This is the state every question begins in, so the multi-answer behavior is something you turn on deliberately rather than something built in from the start.

image.caption: A fresh Multiple Choice question with two blank options and the Multiple answers toggle still switched off.

steps.heading: Flip on Multiple answers
steps.body: Switch the Multiple answers toggle to on, and the option markers immediately change from round radio buttons to square checkboxes — the visible signal that respondents can now select more than one option instead of being locked to a single choice. This one toggle is the entire mechanism; there's no separate question type to hunt for.

steps.heading: Set how many options must be selected
steps.body: Once Multiple answers is on, a new control appears labeled Select total options, with a dropdown offering No limit, Equal to, and At most, paired with a number field. No limit lets a respondent check as many or as few boxes as they want; Equal to forces an exact count, useful for a question where you know precisely how many of the listed items are correct; and At most caps the number they're allowed to check without requiring they hit that number.

image.caption: The Select total options dropdown open, showing No limit, Equal to, and At most as the available constraints on a multi-answer question.

steps.heading: See the finished checkbox layout
steps.body: With Multiple answers on and the total-options rule set, the question settles into its final shape — every option, including any custom Other field you've added, now shows a checkbox instead of a radio button, and the Select total options row stays visible under the option list as a permanent part of the question rather than a one-time setup step you won't see again.

image.caption: The completed multi-answer question with checkboxes on every option and the total-options rule set to No limit.

steps.heading: Add this to a quiz for automatic grading
steps.body: The checkbox mechanics work in any form, but automated correct-answer grading and point values only exist inside the Quiz format. If you're building an assessment rather than a plain survey, make sure you started the project as a quiz, since that's what unlocks marking specific options as correct and assigning a point value once you've finished setting the multi-answer rule.

steps.heading: Turn on Required for questions that can't be skipped
steps.body: The Required toggle sits right next to Multiple answers in the same row, and switching it on stops a respondent from submitting the form without answering that question. For a multi-select scoring question, this matters more than it might for open text — an empty answer under a loose grading setup can otherwise slip through and skew your results.

steps.heading: Preview before you publish
steps.body: Run the Preview option before sharing the quiz with real respondents. It renders the question exactly as they'll see it, so you can click through the checkboxes yourself and confirm the total-options rule behaves the way you expect — for instance, that Equal to actually blocks submission until the right number of boxes are checked.

faq.question: Do I need a quiz instead of a regular form?
faq.answer: Yes — automated correct-answer grading and point values only exist in the Quiz format. The multi-answer checkbox behavior itself works in any form, but scoring requires a quiz.

faq.question: What does the Select total options setting actually control?
faq.answer: It restricts how many checkboxes a respondent can select on a multi-answer question — choose No limit for any number, Equal to for an exact count, or At most for a maximum.

faq.question: Will Multiple Answers work on mobile devices?
faq.answer: Yes — the checkbox layout is responsive, so it's worth using Preview to confirm it displays and behaves correctly on both desktop and mobile before sharing the quiz.

faq.question: Can I go back and edit correct answers after responses come in?
faq.answer: You can edit the answer key at any time, but scores already given won't automatically recalculate unless you go back and review those responses again.

faq.question: How is a multi-answer question different from a regular Multiple Choice question?
faq.answer: The option markers switch from round radio buttons to square checkboxes once you turn on Multiple answers, and a Select total options rule appears to control how many can be checked.
